title: The thousand names held back
hook: Hayagriva leaves out Lalita's thousand names until Agastya asks
carry: a guru guards the practice; devotion opens the door
tomorrow: a city of walls, and red powder at the edge. why start there?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sri Yantra's woven heart: Shiva and Shakti can't be pulled apart. Today, the very center, and a teaching that was almost left out.

The sage Agastya sits at the feet of his teacher, Hayagriva, Vishnu with the head of a horse. Day after day Hayagriva tells him about the Goddess Lalita: how she rose from the gods' sacred fire, the battles she won, the city built for her. Then the teaching ends, and Agastya is troubled. Something is missing: her thousand names. Why leave them out? In the frame of the Lalita Sahasranama, Hayagriva answers: these names are kept close, given only to those who come with devotion. And because you've asked with devotion, I'll give them to you now. So who gets to walk all the way in? People who love this yantra answer two ways.
screen: `AGASTYA LISTENS.` → `THE NAMES ARE MISSING. WHY?` → `KEPT CLOSE, GIVEN TO DEVOTION.`

segments.voice: First, where they're walking to. At the very center of the Sri Yantra sits a dot, the bindu, a drop or a point. One of Lalita's thousand names calls her the one seated in the bindu. The gates, lotuses and woven triangles are rooms of a house; the bindu is where she's at home. Now the two voices. First: in Hinduism the deepest practices pass from guru to student, teacher to disciple, in an unbroken line. In Sri Vidya lineages, the full worship of the yantra and its mantra are received through initiation, called diksha. The best case: the road passes through every layer in order, and someone who has walked it can walk you through. Even Hayagriva didn't hand out the names to just anyone. Second: those same thousand names, once held back, are now chanted in homes and temples everywhere, often by people with no initiation at all. The best case: Agastya was given the names because he asked with devotion, and a mother's house isn't locked to children who ask. Notice what each protects. The first guards the depth. The second guards the welcome. Both rest on one moment: a teacher who guards, and a student who asks with love.
screen: `THE BINDU: WHERE SHE SITS.` · `ONE VOICE: GURU TO STUDENT.` · `DIKSHA: SOMEONE WALKS YOU THROUGH.` · `ANOTHER: HER NAMES SUNG EVERYWHERE.` · then, large: `A GURU GUARDS. DEVOTION ASKS.`

segments.voice: Make a small dot on a piece of paper, or pick one point in front of you. Before you begin, bow your head for a moment to someone who taught you something that mattered; many Hindus begin their practice by honoring their guru. Then let your gaze rest on the point, and let everything around it go soft. Each time the eyes wander, come back to the one point.
The Sri Yantra's center: the bindu, a point with no size, where the Goddess is said to sit and where every line ends.
Your line: a guru guards the practice; devotion opens the door. Agastya asked, and the names were given. Until tomorrow.

DEBATE (two views within Hinduism): Sri Vidya lineages that give the full yantra worship and mantra through diksha, versus household devotion that keeps a yantra and recites the Lalita Sahasranama without initiation. Both steelmanned; neither ranked; 'a mother's house isn't locked to her children' is offered as the open voice's case, not as doctrine. A Sri Vidya teacher should confirm the description of initiation is fair and that nothing here invites anyone to attempt the initiated rite.
